title: Life, Death, Time, Place
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: The talk's main teaching is that true freedom and understanding come from being present in the moment and acknowledging our place in the world. By letting go of attachments and ego, we can tap into a deeper sense of compassion and connection with others and the natural world. Reizan Bob Penny encourages listeners to cultivate this awareness through meditation and mindfulness, reminding them that it's not about achieving some specific state or outcome, but rather about embracing the present moment with an open heart and mind.

sentences.text: Life, death, time, place.
How did we come here?
A long time ago I wrote a poem.
The title was "Today."
*In long ways beyond our sleep we find ourselves walking into another day.
How will we live in this new land around which we were never born?
In lights turned up to meet the face of each wall returning towards us, we will blind ourselves again, walking into a day through a hall where all our own portraits hang, not looking left or right.
So the years will number themselves like leaves on small flights to the ground, and we will know this world was meant for someone else, someone almost ourselves but becoming new again and again.*
Sixty-five years ago, born in Honolulu.
Forty-six years ago, nothing but [unclear: "Philip Kaplow"], whatever thing I could get hold of.

My friend Matt in the university lot went to check out recordings of Alan Watts, because standing in the coffee line in the architecture building I overheard a sentence from a conversation, months before: "Have you ever heard Alan Watts speak?
He has a really [unclear: "mezz..."]."
I heard "Alan Watts, check it out."
That little hallway that went to the listening room went down the only aisle in the whole university library where all the Buddhist books were.

After about ninety seconds, sort of hyperventilating, getting a little bit lightheaded, I thought, "I'm getting enlightened," before my head hit the floor.
So what do you do?
You get up and you try it again.
How did I get there?
Well, one thing is I read this guy.
How did I read him?
Well, I picked up Emerson first, pilfering my parents' bookshelves.
I flipped to the essay "Nature."
I figured it's all about nature.
He said there are things in heaven and earth that are...
I wrote it on a piece of paper and stabbed it with my [unclear: "honey knife"] on my headboard in my bed.
Henry David went to the woods.
He asked why.
He knew where I lived and what I lived for.
The chapter started:
*Let us spend one day as deliberately as nature, and not be thrown off the track by every nutshell, a mosquito's wing that falls on the rails.
Let us rise early and fast, or break fast, gently and without perturbation.
Accompany come and accompany go.
Let the bells ring and the children cry, determined to make a day of it.*
He said he went to the woods.
He wanted to know at the end of his life whether he'd really lived.
That was 1979. 1985, first meditation retreat.
But before that, what happened?
In 1980, road trip, in the dean's car.
We went to New Mexico to show our drawings to some alternative community.
He was from California.
He told us, he told somebody, "Go to this place north of the bay, maybe if you get a chance."
Six a.m.
Where are we going?
Some place north of the bay.
Okay.
We got there by dark.
Somebody met us at the gate and directed us to throw up our tents.
I got up the next morning and everyone was asleep.
I wandered down the road: verandas, walkways, [unclear: "Japaneseque"] buildings, no one there.
The door was open.
Beautiful hall.
I wandered into Green Gulch.
My heart was somehow there, but I tripped over other practices, because I was open to anything.
Sitting in '85 at a Goenka retreat in Massachusetts, what I remember is that at one point in that retreat I felt love, more than I had ever felt love.
At one point in that retreat I felt hate, more than I had ever felt hate.
1987, back at Green Gulch, dropping by for a week's student practice.
Final evening I sit down and have dinner with some guy named Tim.
I'm on this traveling school program.
They want us to look as less hippie as we can, so hair above the ears, clean shaven.
That's the rule.
I'm headed onward to Death Valley, to the southwest, the next day.
It's a chance meeting.
You never think maybe I'll meet this person again.
But a few years later I'm here in Bellingham running environmental life programs.
I need to hire somebody to help me with the day camp.
I have this guy Tim.
We were working together for a couple of weeks.
One day we were on a hike.
We have to ferry a car to this side of the lake, come back around, go back and pick up the car at the end of the day.
I jump in his van.
There's a sticker on the dashboard: Bodhidharma, a sumi brush painting.
I say, "Bodhidharma."
He says, "Bodhidharma [unclear: "Dayosho"]."
We look at each other.
We've met before.
I'm sitting with Three Treasures Sangha in Seattle because, from the east coast, I had called [unclear: "Cocoan Zendo"] and Honolulu: "Do you have any northwest affiliates?"
I had read Robert Aitken's *Mind of Clover*.
They got me in touch.
We traveled around, and somehow I found a couple of practitioners central to their group who actually lived up here.
So I was practicing with them.
But then they lost their teacher, and I was on a committee to help select a new teacher.
And I thought, Norman Fisher.
That guy I met at [unclear: "Green Gorge"] years ago.
He's something.
He's really something.
Norman and I were passing letters back and forth, phone calling.
His final word was, "I just can't see it.
I can't see me coming up and helping establish a sangha."
So later Tim says, "I'm going to start a little sitting group."
He puts up notices.
Little things like this: "Zen sitting, 7 o'clock, my house."
It was me, it was Tim, and his roommate Andrew, on the front porch on Harris Street, glass in porch.
Half the time I didn't come, but every time I'd call, "I can't come."
Even if you're not showing up, looking here.
We take the sauna shack, sweep it out, nail up some drywall, lay down some cushions.
Tim reminded me we had a one-day retreat there, remember?
Oh yeah.
One time the han was hanging over there.
I'd go out early in the morning.
I thought, "I'm just going to give the Meadow a ring."
Tim's in the cabin, newly back from Tassajara.
Here's the call.
He wakes up, he's got his clothes half on, he realizes, "Where am I?"
Ha ha ha.
Nineteen ninety-three, John Robinson's little cabin out there on Lummi Island.
We have our first retreat, Bellingham Zen practice group.
Maybe about this many people, smaller place.
None of us knew anything.
Norman, realizing that we were just fumbling through the whole thing, stepped in as server.
He served us food around to each of our mats.
Giving.
Didn't you die that day?
With Florence.
And Florence, right?
Florence, who sewed the cover from my [unclear: "rocket suit at the mouse"].
Here, 1990, came here.
Thirty-five years, longest person who ever lived here.
All the history, all the way back to John G.
Hyatt Jr., who I told you about, was half Lummi.
All the pioneer men on the bay had native wives.
Some of them were honorable, some of them left.
Given his father's name, they made up a story that he died.
He built the first brick building in Washington State.
It still stands on E Street, half a block.
The story says maybe John G.
Jr. was conceived there.
I had a friend, Tammy.
She was a painter.
Lived in the artist's garret up there.
Some years ago she passed away.
Her paintings are on my wall.
She used to paint on glass, windows, anything she could find, things she couldn't take with her, so she gave them away.
Thirty-five years.
We were out there in the meadow.
There was a history.
Life, death.
Can't even name, although I did name all the animals.
And of course here in the earth, Rose gave her last breath.
You're out there.
Life, death, place.
We sit.
In one square meter we occupy our history.
We need to know where we are, but also where we are.
Twenty-five years ago, twenty-six, I said, "Let's go to the mountain.
Let's walk.
Let's keep it up."
There were years when people said, "Do we have to?"
I said, "Yeah, we have to.
Let's go."
Every year.
And I wanted to keep going long after I'm gone.
That's why I keep going.
Three years, the house was half torn.
We were sleeping in the cabin, spending evenings in front of the wood stove in the house.
Put this little thing in a bassinet, carrying it back and forth.
So many things to say, but sometimes the less said the better.
Last night, sleeping on the ground, you feel Mother Earth accept you.
You feel the reality of place.
When I was in grad school we traveled.
We camped in a different place every night for two years.
Not the religious type, attracted to Native American spirituality but anti-institutional.
But they had a practice, whether they knew it or not.
They decided to sleep on the ground every night, even when they were home at their farms down east.
They didn't use their bedrooms.
They slept out of the earth.
So I aspired to that.
Perhaps some day soon I'll decide, if my body allows, that I'll try to sleep on the ground every day, maybe for a year.
Here, snow, rain.
So, we...
When I was...
I made my own book. [unclear: "Gave me the blank of the glue up he had made"] in shop class with Gary [unclear: "Crabot"], and completed it.
He says it's got twisted limbs.
He wrote it in my yearbook: "Your bow has twisted limbs, unevenly so the string would re-twist them back to the [unclear: "Owl's Sea"]."
Never took a shot at a deer.
It's hard to do.
One night, one late, late afternoon, as evening was getting dark in the forest, I was alone with a deer.
But I could barely tell in the fading light.
I didn't think I should chance it, but you get few chances.
Look at me, quivering, not being able to stay steady.
They call it buck fever.
You want to take a life?
Not want to take a life?
It's a way to move in the world, a way to be how animals are: watchful, aware, sensing, perceptive.
There's a technique in bow hunting, usually in wooded areas.
They call it still hunting.
Very, very slowly, and stopping, like a deer does.
If you notice, they try and trick you.
They're very good at it.
They'll reach down to eat and then they'll look up, see if they caught you moving.
Because most animals can't see color, but they see form, and they see movement.
So don't skyline yourself.
Be a silhouette.
Now, each person can take a cushion, a chair, a bench, one of those tarp mats, [unclear: "Zapatons"] that we have by the door to protect you from the moisture of the ground.
Take your zafu in the mat, all the edges.
Find your spot.
Settle in.
Settle into zazen.
And also, not just looking at that place in front of you, but also, and listen.
Notice what's very near, and notice what's very, very...
When you hear the [unclear: "hawn"], sneak on back.
*[unclear: "Tensions"] equally extend to every being and place, with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, save them.
Delusions are exhaustible, but to mend them, homeless, but to enter them is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
